consumer_seed: The Ofcom ADR guide was published on 8 March 2024.
The Ofcom ADR guide was last updated on 20 July 2026.
A customer should first contact the provider's customer services department and explain the problem.
If customer services does not resolve the problem, the customer should make a formal complaint.
Formal complaint details may be provided on the customer's bill.
Formal complaint details may be provided on the provider's website.
Eligible customers have a right to use an ADR scheme free of charge.
ADR schemes carry out an impartial assessment of complaints.
Residential customers can use ADR when the conditions are met.
Small businesses with up to 10 employees can use ADR when the conditions are met.
Not-for-profit organisations with up to 10 working individuals, excluding volunteers, can use ADR when the conditions are met.
The complaint must already have been raised with the provider.
The complaint must remain unresolved before it is taken to ADR.
A complaint can be taken to ADR after at least six weeks.
A complaint can be taken to ADR earlier when the parties cannot agree and a deadlock letter has been received.
A customer can request a deadlock letter.
The ADR referral must be made less than 12 months after receiving the deadlock letter.
Phone and broadband companies must have an easily accessible complaints code of practice.
The complaints code must set out the provider's complaint-handling process.
The complaints code must provide a phone contact that is free or charged at a geographic-number rate.
The complaints code must provide a postal address.
The complaints code must provide an email address or webform.
The complaints code must describe the steps used to investigate a complaint.
The complaints code must state timeframes for resolving complaints.
The complaints code must explain what customers can do if they remain unhappy, including ADR.
Providers must take prompt and active steps to resolve complaints.
Providers must promptly tell customers the outcome reached.

The Ofcom contract-status guide was published on 12 April 2022.
The Ofcom contract-status guide was last updated on 17 July 2026.
Phone, broadband and pay-TV contracts are typically tied in for 12, 18 or 24 months.
Leaving before a contract ends may trigger an exit fee or early termination charge.
Customers who are out of contract can shop around and may save money by switching.
Customers can ask their provider or check its website or app to see whether they are still in contract.
Providers must tell customers when their contract is coming to an end and provide their best available deals.
Providers must remind customers who remain out of contract every year and update them on their best deals.
End-of-contract notifications may be sent by text, email or letter.
The notification must be sent between 10 and 40 days before the contract ends.
The notification must include the contract end date.
The notification must include any notice period for leaving the provider.
The notification must include the current price and the price payable after the contract ends.
The notification must include the provider's best deals, including prices available only to new customers.
The notification must include details and end dates of other contracts taken as part of a bundle.
The Ofcom new-contract checklist was published on 22 January 2014.
The Ofcom new-contract checklist was last updated on 26 June 2026.
The checklist addresses residential and small-business customers with 10 employees or fewer.
Contracts may be rolling month-to-month arrangements or fixed terms such as 12, 18 or 24 months.
Providers must offer a contract option no longer than 12 months for each service they provide.
A residential or small-business service contract should be no longer than 24 months.
A longer mobile handset contract must be separate from an airtime contract that cannot exceed 24 months.
Early termination charges should not exceed the payments remaining on the contract.
The monthly amount payable should be clearly provided before sign-up.
A price increase beyond what was agreed requires at least one month's notice and a penalty-free exit right.
Specified in-contract rises must state the post-rise amount in pounds and pence and when the rise occurs.
Customers should check usage allowances and charges for exceeding them.
Customers should check extra costs such as paper bills, caller ID, voicemail retrieval or non-direct-debit payment.
Customers should check repair timescales, compensation, other redress and engineer-visit charges.
Ofcom recommends checking price comparison sites accredited by Ofcom.
The Ofcom broadband and landline faults guide was published on 13 October 2023.
The Ofcom broadband and landline faults guide was last updated on 8 April 2026.
Telephone extension leads and wiring changes can cause interference that lowers broadband speed.
Microfilters should be plugged into every telephone socket used in the home.
Electrical devices can interfere with routers, so routers should be kept away from such devices and wireless emitters.
Moving a router from the floor to a table or shelf can improve wireless range.
Additional or thicker walls between the router and devices can reduce broadband speeds.
A phone or broadband service bought online or by phone can be cancelled up to 14 days after entering the contract.
Older routers or outdated router software can cause connection problems.
A provider may be able to detect technical problems by accessing the router remotely.
A provider may ask for a direct Ethernet connection to help establish whether there is a line fault.
Most providers offer an online or app-based service-status checker for known major network problems.
The customer's provider is responsible for ensuring faults are fixed and for keeping the customer updated.
The Ofcom General Conditions page was published on 16 August 2023.
The Ofcom General Conditions page was last updated on 8 April 2026.
All providers of electronic communications networks and services must comply with the General Conditions to provide services in the UK.
The current consolidated General Conditions came into force on 8 April 2026.
The General Conditions are grouped into network functioning, numbering and technical, and consumer protection conditions.
